parts.note: Man is the Isle of Man, whose two senior judges have an old Manx title; the capital at the start hides the island

explanation.surface: A man's own judge, someone who judges him.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M is lost at the start of the clue: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, a self-governing island between Britain and Ireland, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man's high-court justices hold this traditional title.

parts.note: read as a person who lives badly, not a diseased organ

explanation.surface: A diseased liver.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer is someone who lives a wicked life, a bad 'liver' in the sense of one who lives.

definitions.meaning: the phrase 'as a ...' means actually or in truth
plain, unimaginative and practical in manner

explanation.surface: Something real is also dull.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyphenated phrase describes a practical, unemotional manner, and unhyphenated it introduces a statement of what is really so.

indicators.note: a variety is a different arrangement, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Many patterns can be seen inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'in church' points to a part of the building rather than the church itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-arms of a cruciform church building are each one of these wings.

clue.text: Widows' remnants about the end of Lent

indicators.note: the remnants go around the next piece, so one word sits about the other

parts.note: relics are things left over from the past

indicators.note: the last letter of the word Lent is taken

explanation.surface: What widows keep of their husbands at the close of Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe of 'Widows'' is part of the surface; the definition is the plural noun. Lent is the Christian fast before Easter.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a widow is one left behind, a survivor of a dead spouse.

definitions.meaning: the flat side of the skull beside the eye
the Inner and Middle ... are two of London's Inns of Court, where barristers belong

explanation.surface: Barristers get a part in the play at the head of the company.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inns of Court are the professional bodies in London to which every English barrister belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the side of the forehead and a London legal precinct housing barristers' chambers.

clue.text: These hands wanted for light work

definitions.text: These hands wanted for light work

parts.words: These hands wanted for light work
parts.note: plays on the proverb that numerous hands make a job light

explanation.surface: A job advert seeking workers for easy tasks.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says that a large number of helpers make light work of any job.

clue.text: Do these students get paid a pound ?

definitions.text: Do these students get paid a pound ?

parts.words: Do these students get paid a pound ?
parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, so the word splits as people who earn an L

explanation.surface: A question about whether students are given a pound for their work.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for a pound (from Latin libra), so split the answer as L-EARNERS; L is also the plate for a novice driver.
explanation.definitionFit: Students are people being taught, pupils still acquiring a skill.

parts.note: toothsome normally means tasty, but read literally it means having teeth

explanation.surface: Something very far from delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: Edentates are mammals like sloths and anteaters, with few or no teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes animals lacking teeth, the very opposite of being full of them.

definitions.meaning: a regimen of meals set by a doctor
a legislative gathering, such as the parliament of some countries

explanation.surface: Meals ordered for a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a controlled eating plan and a formal legislature, as in the Japanese parliament.

clue.text: Striker who's activities land him in court

definitions.text: Striker who's activities land him in court

parts.words: Striker who's activities land him in court
parts.note: a striker of balls whose game is played on a court, not a worker facing a judge

explanation.surface: A trade-union striker whose actions get him prosecuted.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who plays this racket sport hits the ball on a court.

parts.note: Kipling wrote a Boer War poem about a soldier, called the forgetful beggar

explanation.surface: Asking how foolish the beggar in Kipling's work was.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 1899 poem 'The Absent-Minded Beggar' raised money for soldiers' families.
explanation.definitionFit: Being forgetful and preoccupied is to have one's mind elsewhere, a kind of empty-headedness.

clue.text: With which to shell out in the Indian Ocean?

definitions.text: With which to shell out in the Indian Ocean?

parts.words: With which to shell out in the Indian Ocean?
parts.note: shell out means pay, and these sea shells were used as money around the Indian Ocean

explanation.surface: Asking how one pays bills when out in the Indian Ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: These glossy sea-snail shells served as currency in parts of Asia and Africa.

parts.note: insularity is read as being an island, which gave Stevenson's book its title

explanation.surface: Something whose isolation made it new and original.
explanation.walkthrough: R. L. Stevenson's novel is 'Treasure Island': adding the island makes the novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Valuable hoard, which joined to the word island names Stevenson's pirate adventure book.

indicators.note: letters reorganized are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Money made from a sport once it is restructured.
explanation.definitionFit: Financial returns or earnings are what a business gains.

parts.note: the birds of the tropical family named after heaven

explanation.surface: A place that is bliss for birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven itself, and the name of the brilliantly plumed birds of New Guinea.

parts.note: keys open locks, and in cricket the first pair of batsmen start the innings

explanation.surface: The most important batsmen in a cricket team.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the two batsmen who begin a side's innings share the name with things that open, such as keys.
explanation.definitionFit: Tools that open things, and the first two batters in a cricket innings, share this name.

clue.text: This cape may be an imitation

indicators.note: suggests these letters may be something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A cloak that might be a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: A work imitating the style of another artist or period.

parts.note: uncommonly means extremely, but also literally means by not being common

explanation.surface: Things that might be extremely precious.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare objects are valuable precisely because they are seldom found.

clue.text: Poor Lorna Doone losing one lover in Arden

indicators.note: poor suggests the letters are in a bad state and need rearranging

explanation.surface: The heroine of the novel Lorna Doone loses a sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes the letters of ONE from LORNA DOONE, and 'Poor' rearranges LORNAD O. The Forest of Arden is the setting of Shakespeare's 'As You Like It'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosalind's suitor in Shakespeare's forest comedy 'As You Like It'.

definitions.meaning: a servant or attendant kept in a household
a payment made in advance to secure a lawyer's services

explanation.surface: The fee charged by a keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an old family servant and an advance payment that secures a professional's services.

definitions.meaning: ... Eddy, the American singer and film star
Admiral Lord ... won the Battle of the Nile in 1798

explanation.surface: A swirl of water on the Nile.
explanation.definitionFit: First name of singer Eddy, and surname of the admiral made Baron of the Nile.

clue.text: The doctor vexed about appearing gloomy

indicators.note: the vexed word goes around the doctor

parts.note: sore means annoyed or vexed
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: The doctor is annoyed about seeming depressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark and melancholy, dismal in mood.

clue.text: This operation is intended to promote a good spirit

definitions.text: This operation is intended to promote a good spirit

parts.words: This operation is intended to promote a good spirit
parts.note: spirit is read as strong liquor, made by boiling and condensing

explanation.surface: An activity meant to boost morale.
explanation.definitionFit: The process of vaporizing and condensing that produces whisky and other spirits.

indicators.note: doubly means two times over, so the word meaning thus is written out twice in a row

parts.note: so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: Being thus twice over means being lukewarm.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediocre, neither good nor bad.

clue.text: It could be said to improve one's standing

definitions.text: It could be said to improve one's standing

parts.words: It could be said to improve one's standing
parts.note: standing read literally as height, which a platform raises

explanation.surface: Something that boosts social status.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised platform lifts whoever stands on it above the floor.

clue.text: Does it cause a hold-up in window-dressing?

definitions.text: Does it cause a hold-up in window-dressing?

parts.words: Does it cause a hold-up in window-dressing?
parts.note: hold-up read as holding up a window, not a delay

explanation.surface: Asking whether something delays the decorating of shop windows.
explanation.definitionFit: The rope over a pulley that holds a sliding sash window up.

parts.note: W. G. Grace was a doctor and cricketer, so he might give a cricket over and a dose of medicine

explanation.surface: Complaining that the doctor has prescribed excessively.
explanation.walkthrough: W. G. Grace, the great Victorian cricketer, was also a medical doctor; an over is six balls bowled in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: An excessive amount of a drug, here split as a cricket over plus a medical dose.
